strengths: Unifies gradient-based token attribution (Integrated Gradients) with contrastive activation steering in a single framework applicable to both LLMs and VLMs, addressing a real limitation of prior work that uses fixed, global steering directions or relies on external modality-specific heuristics (e.g., object detectors).

Broad and consistent empirical evaluation across five base models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B-IT) and multiple safety-relevant benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL), with comparisons against strong recent steering baselines (ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT) and LoRA fine-tuning.

Careful attention to preserving general capabilities (MMLU, MMMU, BLEU-based generation quality), showing GRAInS largely avoids the capability degradation exhibited by several baselines (e.g., CAA's large MMLU/MMMU drops).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the attribution method (IG vs. vanilla gradients vs. SmoothGrad vs. random selection), modality balance (vision-only vs. text-only vs. joint), the preference-based vs. likelihood-based attribution objective, and hyperparameters (steering strength, top-k tokens).

Reasonable efficiency argument (runtime of steering vector construction vs. LoRA fine-tuning) supporting the practicality claim, along with qualitative examples illustrating behavior differences from baselines.
weaknesses: No reported variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing across the many benchmark results; several reported differences between GRAInS and the strongest baseline are small (e.g., <1% on some VLM/LLM metrics), making it hard to assess robustness of the claimed improvements.

Key reproducibility details are underspecified in the main text, such as which/how many transformer layers receive the steering intervention, how σ and k are jointly tuned per task/model (tuning appears to be done mainly on TruthfulQA/SPA-VL and then possibly reused), and how sensitive results are to the 50-sample steering set size.

The method still requires curated preference pairs (y_pos/y_neg) to construct attribution and steering vectors; while an ablation shows a single-reference variant works, its performance is consistently worse, so the core method's lightweight claim is somewhat tempered by this supervision requirement.

Some baseline results look surprisingly poor (e.g., CAA causing a 17.78% MMLU drop, 17.13% MMMU drop), raising the possibility that baselines were not fully optimized for these particular settings/backbones, which would inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

Generation-quality preservation is measured only via a BLEU-based proxy metric (closer to preferred vs. dispreferred response) rather than human evaluation or a more standard quality/fluency metric, limiting the strength of the 'preserves fluency' claim.

The technical contribution is primarily a careful engineering combination of existing techniques (Integrated Gradients, contrastive activation differences, PCA aggregation) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism, which may temper novelty relative to the extensive empirical claims made.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: existing inference-time steering methods for LLMs/VLMs apply uniform, global interventions that ignore which specific tokens (visual or textual) actually drive undesirable behavior; GRAINS offers a principled fix by using contrastive Integrated Gradients to identify influential tokens before constructing steering vectors.

Very thorough empirical evaluation spanning both language-only (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) and multimodal (LLaVA-1.6-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) settings, across multiple benchmarks (TruthfulQA, Toxigen, FaithEval, MMHal-Bench, SPA-VL) and multiple strong baselines (LoRA, ICV, NL-ITI, CAA, VTI, ICT, RUDDER, SHARP).

Extensive and well-designed ablation studies: effect of k (number of attributed tokens), attribution method comparison (IG vs. vanilla gradients, SmoothGrad, random selection), PCA vs. mean aggregation, layer-wise and token-wise steering choices, normalization step, and modality-specific (vision-only vs. text-only) attribution — these substantially strengthen the soundness and interpretability of the design choices.

Demonstrates that the method preserves general capabilities (MMLU, MMMU, BLEU-based fluency) much better than baselines that often degrade them, which is an important and often-overlooked property for steering methods.

Additional generalization experiments (cross-dataset transfer to RealToxicityPrompts and POPE, scaling to a 72B VLM) and a computational overhead analysis (throughput drop <5%) add credibility to the claimed practicality and robustness of the approach.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, dataset/model licensing, prompts, and code availability are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the core pipeline combines well-established components (Integrated Gradients, PCA-based contrastive direction extraction akin to CAA/ICV, norm-preserving injection) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the main innovation is selective token identification via attribution, which, while useful, is a relatively modest technical step.

The main results rely on paired preference data (y_pos/y_neg) to compute attribution; although a single-reference ablation is reported, most headline numbers assume access to labeled preferred/dispreferred outputs, which may not be a realistic constraint for all steering use-cases and is not strongly emphasized as a limitation in the main text.

No variance/robustness analysis across seeds or repeated runs is reported; given that steering vectors are built from only 50 samples, and hyperparameters (λ, k) are model- and dataset-specific (Fig. 5–6 show different optima for Llama vs. Qwen), the sensitivity of results to these choices and to sampling variance is not well characterized.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully transparent — it is unclear whether baselines received comparable hyperparameter tuning effort/budget as GRAINS, especially for methods like CAA and LoRA that show unusually large capability degradation (e.g., 17% MMLU/MMMU drops), which raises questions about whether these baselines are optimally configured.

The requirement to select λ per model/task (with no automatic or adaptive scheme, explicitly left to future work) and the acknowledged 'undercorrection' failure mode suggest the method's practical robustness across arbitrary tasks/domains is not fully established.

Some evaluation choices (e.g., SPA-VL preference measured via log-likelihood chosen>rejected rather than actual generated outputs) may not fully capture real-world generation quality improvements, and qualitative analysis, while illustrative, is based on only a handful of hand-picked examples.
